common_name: Dark Ponticum Bee Balm (Blue-Green Foliage Purple Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil and full sun; the blue-green foliage colors best with consistent moisture through summer.

directions: Dark Ponticum is a Monarda selection prized for its blue-green foliage, a cooler-toned backdrop that few other bee balms offer, topped by abundant violet-purple flower heads in early summer. In side-by-side trials at Mt. Cuba Center it produced an unusually long and full bloom display, holding near-full flower coverage for roughly three weeks, and while powdery mildew can appear on the leaves late in the season it rarely causes the yellowing or leaf drop seen in less resistant cultivars. Plant in average to moist, well-drained garden soil and give it full sun for the tightest habit and best flowering; part-day shade is tolerated but can encourage stem stretch. Divide the clump every few years in spring to maintain vigor and keep the planting from crowding itself out.

planting.note: Plant in spring into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; dry summer soil increases the risk of powdery mildew.

directions: On Parade is an older Monarda selection valued for its brilliant orchid-purple flower heads, a shade distinct from the more common scarlet and rosy-pink bee balms. Growing to around four feet tall, it has shown fair resistance to powdery mildew in regional trial gardens, performing comparably to other reliable purple-flowered selections rather than standing out as mildew-proof. Give it full sun and consistently moist, fertile soil, since dry conditions in mid-summer raise the odds of foliar disease. As with most bee balms, deadheading spent flower heads tidies late-season appearance and dividing the clump every two to three years keeps the planting from becoming congested.

common_name: Pink Lace Bee Balm (Compact Pink Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant in spring in rich, evenly moist soil; its compact size suits small borders and rain gardens better than taller bee balms.

directions: Pink Lace is a distinctly compact bee balm, reaching only about a foot to a foot and a half tall and wide, which makes it useful for smaller borders or front-of-bed plantings where taller Monarda didyma cultivars would overwhelm the space. It blooms from early to late summer with clear pink flower heads that draw hummingbirds and butterflies in the same way as its larger relatives. Grow it in rich, evenly moist to wet soil in full sun to part shade, since its compact root system is less drought-tolerant than larger bee balms, and a bit of afternoon shade helps it through hot summer stretches. It tolerates clay and periodically wet soil well, making it a good fit for rain gardens and low spots that stay moist.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun; divide every few years to keep the spreading clump in bounds.

directions: Twins is a mid-sized Monarda cultivar listed by the Royal Horticultural Society, growing roughly two to three feet tall with clear pink, shaggy flower heads around two inches across held above the aromatic foliage. Like other bee balms it spreads by shallow rhizomes to form a slowly expanding colony, so give it room or plan to divide it every few years to keep it within bounds. Plant in full sun in moist, humus-rich soil for the densest flowering and best disease resistance, since soil that dries out in summer tends to bring on powdery mildew earlier in the season. The nectar-rich flowers are a strong draw for bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies through the mid-summer bloom period.

common_name: Violet Queen Bee Balm (Mildew-Resistant Purple Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this vigorous grower is a strong bee magnet true to its name.

directions: Violet Queen carries large, shaggy purple flower heads on plants reaching about four feet tall, with individual flowers measuring roughly three inches across at peak bloom in early summer. Its leaves have a fine coating of silvery hairs that gives the foliage a dull, slightly gray-green cast similar to wild bergamot (Monarda fistulosa), and in multi-year trials it showed excellent resistance to powdery mildew, staying clean through the hottest part of the season. Plant in full sun to light shade in average to moist, well-drained soil; it is a vigorous grower and a strong bee magnet. Divide congested clumps in spring every few years to maintain airflow through the foliage and sustain the plant's naturally good disease resistance.
